title: What is Open-Session-In-View (OSIV)? Why does it hide LazyInitializationException, and why is it discouraged in production?
shortTitle: What is Open-Session-In-View and why disable it?
topicTitle: Performance: Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV
keyPoints: OSIV keeps the Hibernate Session open for the entire HTTP request, including view rendering and JSON serialization.
Because the session stays open during rendering, lazy associations can still be loaded, which hides LazyInitializationException.
Spring Boot enables OSIV by default via OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor to reduce beginner friction.
OSIV causes N+1 queries during serialization because each lazy association fires a separate SELECT outside the transaction.
OSIV holds the database connection for the whole request, exhausting the connection pool faster under load.
OSIV blurs transaction boundaries because lazy selects run after the transaction commits, in auto-commit mode.
Disable OSIV with spring.jpa.open-in-view=false and fetch exactly what you need in the service layer using JOIN FETCH or DTO projections.

s1_definition.oneliner: OSIV keeps the persistence context open through view rendering so lazy loads work during serialization, hiding LazyInitializationException, but it leaks database access into the view and causes N+1 queries.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Open-Session-In-View (OSIV)** -- a pattern that keeps the Hibernate Session open for the entire HTTP request, not just the service-layer transaction.
- **Enabled by default** -- Spring Boot enables it via `OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor` to reduce beginner friction.
- **Hides LazyInitializationException** -- because the session stays open during rendering, lazy associations load on demand instead of throwing an exception.
- **N+1 queries** -- each lazy association Jackson touches during serialization fires a separate SELECT, outside the transaction.
- **Connection held** -- the database connection stays associated with the request through rendering, exhausting the pool faster under load.
- **Blurred boundaries** -- lazy selects run after the transaction has committed, in auto-commit mode, which is confusing and hides performance issues.
s1_definition.analogy: OSIV is like keeping the bank vault at National Bank of India open from the moment Priya walks in until she has walked all the way out and finished reading her printed statement in the lobby -- not just while Rajesh is actively serving her at the counter. It is convenient because Priya can ask for one more detail while reading in the lobby. But the vault is open far too long, Rajesh gets pulled away for ad-hoc lookups outside the controlled session, and the clean "service done, vault closed" boundary is lost.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Request lifecycle WITH OSIV:

  Request ──► Filter opens Session
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @Transactional Service Layer     │
  │  - Load Account (SELECT)          │
  │  - Transaction COMMITS            │
  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                 │  Session still open!
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Controller / Jackson             │
  │  - Serialize Account to JSON      │
  │  - Touch lazy transactions        │
  │  - N+1 SELECTs fire here!         │
  │  - OUTSIDE the transaction        │
  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  Filter closes Session, connection returned


  Request lifecycle WITHOUT OSIV:

  Request ──►
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @Transactional Service Layer     │
  │  - Load Account with JOIN FETCH   │
  │  - Build DTO                      │
  │  - Session closes at TX end       │
  │  - Connection returned to pool    │
  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Controller / Jackson             │
  │  - Serialize DTO (no proxies)     │
  │  - No database access             │
  │  - No connection held             │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Open-Session-In-View keeps the Hibernate Session open for the entire HTTP request, including JSON serialization, so lazy associations load on demand instead of throwing `LazyInitializationException`. Spring Boot enables it by default to reduce beginner friction. But in production it causes N+1 queries during serialization, holds database connections through the entire response, and blurs transaction boundaries by running lazy selects after the transaction has committed.

The fix is to set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` and fetch exactly what each endpoint needs inside the transactional service layer using JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, or DTO projections. These approaches make the data-loading explicit, predictable, and efficient. `LazyInitializationException` after disabling OSIV is not a problem to work around -- it is a signal that the fetch strategy needs to be fixed.

At National Bank of India, the customer detail endpoint returned an Account with a lazy list of transactions. With OSIV on, Jackson loaded them one lazy call at a time, producing an N+1 storm that only surfaced as slowness and connection pool exhaustion under peak traffic. Rajesh disabled OSIV, rewrote the endpoint to return a DTO built from a single JOIN FETCH query inside a read-only transaction, and the N+1 problem disappeared.

Remember one sentence: disable OSIV on day one and fetch what you need explicitly in the service layer -- `LazyInitializationException` is a signal to fix the fetch, not re-enable OSIV.
